title.narrative: Plan International Sverige Digital Skills 4 Youth 2023-2026
Plan International Sweden Digital Skills 4 Youth 2023-2026

description.narrative: Ansökan om finansieringsstöd från Plan International Sverige för ett projekt med titeln ”Digital Skills 4 Youth Project 2023-2026”, syftar till att utforma ett program för ungdomars anställbarhet och entreprenörskap underbyggt av digitala färdigheter med olika tvärsektoriella och urban-landsbygdskopplingar.

The application for funding support by Plan International Sweden for a project titled Digital Skills 4 Youth Project 2023-2026, seeks to model a youth employability and entrepreneurship programme underpinned by digital skills with various cross-sectoral and urban-rural linkages.

The broad outcome of the proposal is to enhance sustainable, productive economic development for youth, particularly young women in a supportive environment for digital skills entrepreneurship and employment in targeted areas. The intervention has identified outcomes as key in achieving the set objective:
Outcome 1
1,680 young people, including young women in the targeted areas have strengthened skills relevant for the digital labour market. An additional 3000 young people will be reached under the virtual market intervention.
Outcome 2
Targeted areas have strengthened structures for young people's professional development including linkages with the digital labour market, especially for young women
Outcome 3
Private and governmental sectors on a national and local level have taken actions to enhance young womens economic rights and economic participation
Young women in Zimbabwe face high rates of unemployment coupled with its negative effects including lack of livelihood, and high rates of negative coping mechanisms (e.g. crime, drug abuse and risky health behaviours). There is a huge digital divide in Zimbabwe that cannot be ignored if digital skills programmes are to be truly equitable. Thus, the intervention is expected to impact young peoples digital skills, enabling their sustainable income-generation through either entrepreneurship or employment.
The project offers two streams of digital skills interventions; that is, tailored for rural and urban youth. It is envisaged that the basic digital skills stream coupled with the MakerSpace model (physical work spaces equipped to provide technical training on agro-processing that incorporates basic digital skills) will enable rural youth to perform ICT-enhanced trade through entrepreneurship or employment; whilst the intermediate/advanced digital skills stream coupled with the job market linkages will enhance urban youths employability or entrepreneurship in the digital economy.

Introduction
The digital skills for youth is a 3-year project running upto 2026 with SEK 40 million support from the Embassy. The initiative led by Plan International and its partners has made some progress in transforming the lives of young peopleespecially young womenacross targeted regions in Zimbabwe. Despite facing several structural challenges throughout the year, the project, built around three core outcomes, managed to make traction towards attaining its objectives.
Outcome 1: Strengthened Digital Skills for Youth
-This training opened new pathways for employment and entrepreneurship, especially for young women who had previously faced barriers to entering the digital economy. Many participants reported increased confidence in using digital tools, improved job readiness, and a clearer understanding of how to monetize their skills in online and local markets. Participants reported making income designing marketing posters and preparing CVs. Others were employed as agents for mobile money kiosk and agents for funeral insurances in their communities.
-Additionally, 930 youth (589 female, 341 male) received soft and life skills training, including business mentoring. These sessions helped participants develop critical thinking, communication, and entrepreneurial skillsessential for navigating both formal employment and self-employment. The integration of life skills with digital training ensured a holistic approach to youth empowerment. This has further laid a foundation necessary for job placements in the coming months which Plan International will be facilitating.
Outcome 2: Strengthened Structures for Professional Development
-The second outcome focused on creating enabling environments for youth development. The refurbishment and operationalization of five digital hubs in Harare, Bulawayo, Mutare, Tsholotsho, and Chiredzi marked a significant milestone. These hubs, equipped with trainers and digital infrastructure, became safe and inclusive spaces for learning, innovation, and collaboration. Participants have been organized into value chain based cooperative groups such as vegetables, oil processing and soap making. Registration of cooperatives and food safety approval are underway.
-The partnership with a local university to develop curricula and train trainers ensured that the content was both relevant and sustainable. In rural areas, the inclusion of Makerspaces within the hubs allowed youth to engage in small-scale production, fostering innovation and practical application of skills. The youth are still to realise income from the production centres once they have recieved food safety approvals.
-These hubs not only provided access to technology but also served as community anchors for youth engagement, mentorship, and networking. Young women benefited from the safe and supportive environments, which encouraged their participation and leadership in digital spaces. E-commerce platform has been developed and Plan has begun its operationalization to ensure that youth are connected with relevant employers. furthermore, a consultant has been engaged to assist with job placements and fares providing a critical link to job markets.
Outcome 3: Institutional Support for Young Womens Economic Rights
-The third outcome aimed at influencing systemic change by engaging the private and public sectors. Through advocacy and collaboration, the project encouraged stakeholders to take concrete actions to support young womens economic participation. This was achieved through policy dialogues, awareness campaigns, and the integration of gender-sensitive approaches in employment and entrepreneurship trainings. As a result, there was a noticeable shift in attitudes and practices among local institutions. Employers began to recognize the value of digital skills and the potential of young women as contributors to the digital economy. Some local businesses even partnered with the hubs to offer internships and job placements, further bridging the gap between training and employment. For example, Tubelihle Ndebele, 21 year old girl in Tsholotsho after completing her course on basic digital skills got a job as an ecocash agent and credits the communication and digital skills she learnt at the hub.
-To capture and amplify the projects impact, work began on a documentary showcasing the stories of transformation, innovation, and resilience among the youth. This documentary aims to inspire further investment in youth digital empowerment and highlight the importance of sustainable, inclusive development.
Challenges
While the digital skills initiative made progress in empowering youthparticularly young womenwith relevant digital and life skills, several critical shortcomings have emerged in the reports and field visits made throughout the year that threaten the full realization of the projects intended impact. These gaps, if not addressed urgently, risk undermining the sustainability and long-term success of the initiative.
-Two years into the project, the pace of implementation remains a significant concern. Despite the successful enrollment of youth in training programs, many have yet to transition into job placements or income-generating activities. The MakerSpaces, leather cluster, and job linkage componentscentral to the project's economic empowerment goalsremain largely inactive. This delay has created a disconnect between skills acquisition and practical application, leaving many beneficiaries in a state of limbo, unable to translate their training into tangible economic benefits.
-The lack of timely job placements and income opportunities not only dampens the morale of participants but also risks eroding trust in the programs promises. For many young people, especially in rural areas, the expectation of immediate or near-term economic improvement was a key motivator for participation. Access to finance for starting businesses remains a challenge. The absence of follow-through in this regard has created frustration and uncertainty.
-Another major shortcoming lies in the absence of a clear and actionable sustainability plan. Two years into project implementation, Plan International is still to come up with a sustainability plan and begin implementation. Critical elements like cooperative registrations and food safety approvals remain pending.
-Furthermore, the financial sustainability of some work spaces especially in urban areas due to high rental costs is questionable, with operational costs likely to become unmanageable once donor funding ends. This lack of foresight threatens the longevity of the hubs and the continuity of services for youth. Without a sustainability framework, the risk is high that the infrastructure and momentum built during the project period will dissipate, leaving communities without lasting benefits.
-Several strategic components outlined in Plan Internationals original proposal remain unimplemented. Notably, the mapping of potential Swedish private sector actors by Plan HQ has not materialized. This mapping was intended to facilitate mentorships, internships, and job opportunities. Similarly, the anticipated collaboration with 34 companies to develop minimum viable products has not progressed, limiting the scope for innovation and market integration.
-Moreover, the proposal highlighted the value of leveraging existing Impact Hub networks and private sector partnerships for rapid youth engagement. However, these linkages have not been fully activated. The envisioned quarterly engagement of a project consultant to support these efforts has also not been realized, further weakening the projects strategic execution.
-The project was designed to build on lessons learned from previous initiatives, such as the WFP-funded Digital Skills programme and the Impact Hub Micro Workspace model. However, the scaling of these tested models has been limited. The absence of structured internships and job fairsdespite being integral to the curriculum designhas further constrained the transition from training to employment.
-These missed opportunities represent not just implementation gaps but also a failure to capitalize on proven strategies that could have accelerated impact and enhanced credibility with stakeholders.
Have all these been put in place during the 2 years of implementation the project could have realised even more tangible results to date.
